questionText: Ever since the argument, Nuria has been pointedly unfriendly towards him.
targetSentence: Ever since the argument, Nuria has ____ him.
explanation: 'Give someone the cold shoulder' needs the definite article and the indirect object before it. Candidates often write 'given the cold shoulder to him', which is possible but wastes a word and frequently breaks the limit.

questionText: At the last minute the buyer became too nervous to go through with the purchase.
targetSentence: At the last minute the buyer ____ and pulled out of the purchase.
explanation: 'Get cold feet' takes no article and no possessive, and 'feet' is invariably plural. The frequent error is 'got cold foot' or the insertion of 'his'.

questionText: The unpredictable questions from the audience kept the panel alert all evening.
targetSentence: The unpredictable questions from the audience ____ all evening.
correctAnswer: kept the panel on their toes
explanation: 'Keep someone on their toes' requires the possessive determiner agreeing with the object, not the subject. Learners commonly write 'on the toes' or 'in their toes'.

questionText: As a rough general principle, you should allow an hour for each section.
targetSentence: ____, you should allow an hour for each section.
explanation: 'As a rule of thumb' is a frozen sentence adverbial with the indefinite article. Candidates writing 'As the rule of thumb' or 'By a rule of thumb' lose the mark despite conveying the meaning.

questionText: There is something wrong with the recording, but I cannot identify exactly what it is.
targetSentence: There is something wrong with the recording, but I cannot ____.
correctAnswer: quite put my finger on it
explanation: 'Put one's finger on it' retains the object pronoun, which candidates routinely delete because the target sentence ends there. The possessive must agree with the subject.

questionText: The demonstration became completely impossible to control within minutes.
targetSentence: The demonstration ____ within minutes.
explanation: 'Get out of hand' takes no article before 'hand', which is what distinguishes it from the literal 'out of the hand'. The adverb carries 'completely' across from the lead sentence.

questionText: The repairs to the roof turned out to be extremely expensive indeed.
targetSentence: The repairs to the roof ____.
correctAnswer: cost an arm and a leg
explanation: The idiom is frozen with both indefinite articles; omitting the second gives the ungrammatical 'an arm and leg'. 'Cost' is unchanged in the past tense, which candidates sometimes over-correct to 'costed'.

questionText: Do not take him seriously — he is only joking with you.
targetSentence: Do not take him seriously — he is only ____.
explanation: 'Pull someone's leg' requires the possessive determiner and keeps 'leg' singular. The continuous form is fixed by 'is only' already in the target sentence.

questionText: My supervisor has been monitoring my every move all week.
targetSentence: My supervisor has been ____ all week.
explanation: 'Breathe down someone's neck' takes the possessive of the person being watched, not the watcher. Candidates often reverse it and write 'breathing down his neck'.

questionText: The funding fell through, so the team had to start again from the very beginning.
targetSentence: The funding fell through, so the team was ____.
explanation: 'Back to square one' takes the numeral, not the article: 'square one', never 'the first square'. No preposition follows, which is what makes the three-word answer complete.

questionText: After months of simmering tension, the dispute finally reached a crisis point.
targetSentence: After months of simmering tension, the dispute finally ____.
explanation: 'Come to a head' takes the indefinite article and is intransitive, so nothing follows it. Learners often write 'came to the head', which reads as a literal movement.

questionText: The police were following the suspects extremely closely at that point.
targetSentence: At that point the police were ____ the suspects.
explanation: 'Hot on the heels of' is fixed and requires the plural 'heels' plus 'of' before the noun phrase. Candidates frequently drop 'hot', which leaves a phrase meaning simply 'behind'.

questionText: It took Marta a whole term to overcome her shyness and start talking in class.
targetSentence: It took Marta a whole term to ____ and start talking in class.
explanation: 'Come out of one's shell' needs the possessive agreeing with the subject. The commonest slip is 'come out of the shell', which turns a metaphor about character into a literal statement.

questionText: After a decade in the same post, Xavier felt his career had become utterly monotonous.
targetSentence: After a decade in the same post, Xavier felt he ____.
correctAnswer: had got stuck in a rut
explanation: 'In a rut' takes the indefinite article and follows 'stuck' or 'get'. Candidates often write 'in the rut', which loses the idiomatic reading of stagnation.

questionText: By hesitating for a fortnight, they lost their opportunity entirely.
targetSentence: By hesitating for a fortnight, they ____ entirely.
explanation: 'Miss the boat' takes the definite article and is fixed in the singular. The verb cannot be replaced by 'lose', which is what the Spanish 'perder' invites.

questionText: The second goal completely reversed the momentum of the match.
targetSentence: The second goal completely ____ the match.
explanation: 'Turn the tide of something' needs the definite article and 'of' before the noun. Learners regularly omit 'of' and produce an ungrammatical juxtaposition of two noun phrases.

questionText: Their old quarrel is no longer of the slightest importance to anyone.
targetSentence: As far as anyone is concerned, their old quarrel is ____ now.
explanation: The idiom takes no article at all before 'water', which is uncountable here. Candidates writing 'the water under the bridge' turn a set phrase into a literal description.

questionText: We will deal with that particular problem when it actually arises.
targetSentence: We will ____ when we come to it.
explanation: The proverb is fixed as 'cross that bridge when we come to it', with the demonstrative rather than the definite article. Candidates who write 'cross the bridge' lose the idiomatic force.

questionText: The minister has been severely criticised over the leaked documents.
targetSentence: The minister has ____ over the leaked documents.
explanation: 'Come under fire' takes no article, and the preposition governing the cause is 'over' or 'for'. The frequent error is 'come under the fire', which reads literally.

questionText: Someone had to say something to relieve the awkwardness at the start of the evening.
targetSentence: Someone had to ____ at the start of the evening.
explanation: 'Break the ice' is fixed with the definite article and no following complement. Candidates sometimes write 'broke the ices' or add 'up', neither of which exists.

questionText: Campaigners fear the exemption is only the first step towards far wider deregulation.
targetSentence: Campaigners fear the exemption is ____ far wider deregulation.
correctAnswer: the thin end of the wedge
explanation: The idiom needs both definite articles and the adjective 'thin'; without it the phrase means nothing. Note that no preposition follows in this frame, since the wedge itself stands for what is coming.

questionText: The company survived the financial crisis remarkably well.
targetSentence: The company ____ remarkably well.
explanation: 'Weather the storm' is the fixed verb-noun pair, and the modifier from the lead sentence must be carried inside it. Learners often reach for 'survived', which is precisely the word the transformation is replacing.

questionText: However bad the setback, there is usually something positive to be found in it.
targetSentence: However bad the setback, there is usually ____ to be found in it.
explanation: 'A silver lining' takes the indefinite article; the full proverb 'every cloud has a silver lining' is not needed here. Candidates often supply the whole saying and exceed the word limit.

questionText: Somehow the press found out about the resignation before it was announced.
targetSentence: Somehow the press ____ the resignation before it was announced.
explanation: 'Get wind of' takes no article before 'wind' and requires 'of'. The frequent error is 'got the wind of', which sounds literal and is marked wrong.

questionText: The unexpected apology completely deflated his indignation.
targetSentence: The unexpected apology completely ____.
correctAnswer: took the wind out of his sails
explanation: The idiom is long but frozen: definite article, 'out of', and the possessive before the plural 'sails'. At seven words it sits near the limit, so any added word makes the answer unmarkable.
